title: BFloat16 reduction sensitivity and fallback protocols
content:
Purpose and high-level summary:
This note documents a focused investigation into numerical sensitivity when using bfloat16 (bf16) reductions and accumulation paths in the serving runtime. The goal is to: (1) characterize failure modes that lead to NaNs or extreme divergence in outputs, (2) outline lightweight runtime detection heuristics, and (3) propose a deterministic fallback protocol (bf16 -> fp32) that minimizes latency and cost impact while preserving correctness for production requests.

Motivation and scope:
- We have seen intermittent customer incidents where a small subset of requests produces NaN tokens or incoherent logits when served on bf16-optimized kernels. These are rare but high-impact for production latency and trust.
- This doc focuses on reduction/accumulation sites (GEMM reductions, layer norm moments, softmax numerics) and interactions with the KV cache and scheduler (batched vs single-request execution). We do NOT re-evaluate model architecture-level fixes (e.g., rescaling weights) here — scope is runtime mitigations and detection.

Observed failure classes (summary of experiments):
1) Transient NaN spike after large attention window growth. Reproduction pattern: long prompt (>2k tokens aggregated across batched requests) + sudden request with outlier token distribution (very large logits). Outcome: single-step NaN in attention reduce due to intermediate denorm/inf accumulation.
2) Gradual drift in softmax normalization when accumulation uses bf16 intermediate sums across long sequences and continuous batching. Small bias accumulates into logit scale, causing downstream sampling to prefer degenerate token sequences after ~100 tokens.
3) KV cache replay amplification: when a cached KV tensor was computed with bf16 and later used with a fp32 query (mixed path due to routing), mismatched dynamic ranges cause local underflow/overflow in fused kernels.

Key empirical findings (microbench highlights):
- Turning accumulation to fp32 (only for reduction axis) eliminates NaN reproductions in our harness for all tested inputs, at ~5-12% additional token latency depending on sequence length and kernel implementation.
- Selective fp32 fallback limited to: GEMM reduction (col sum) + softmax accumulator + layernorm moment sum recovers correctness in 99.8% of cases tested.
- Full fp32 everywhere is costly (~2x token-level latency on some GPU configs) and unnecessary; targeted fallbacks are sufficient.

Root cause hypotheses: technical summary
- bf16 has 8 exponent bits vs fp32's 8 (bf16 same exponent range as fp32) but only 7 mantissa bits; large dynamic range events and accumulation over large fan-in cause catastrophic precision loss. In fused kernels that accumulate in bf16 with many summands, round-off error and denorm handling interact with hardware flushing to zero or producing NaN in later ops (divide-by-zero after subtraction yields NaN).
- Kernel fusion hides intermediate normalization steps that would otherwise stabilize values if computed in higher precision.
- Mixed execution paths (e.g., some components of the request run on a fallback path while cached KVs were produced in bf16) creates heterogeneous numeric assumptions.

Detection heuristics (runtime checks):
We propose lightweight, low-overhead checks that detect signs of numerical instability early in the token generation pipeline. These are intentionally conservative and designed to avoid false positives that would trigger costly fallbacks. The checks are implemented as optional flags in the runtime config.
- Infinity/NaN short-circuit: after key reduction points (post-GEMM reduction, pre-softmax, post-attention), assert isfinite(tensor) on a small sample of elements (for performance, sample 8–32 uniformly-chosen lanes). If any sample detects NaN/Inf -> trigger fallback.
- Dynamic range anomaly score: compute (max_abs / median_abs) on sampled lanes; if score > threshold (e.g., 1e6) -> consider fallback. This targets outlier logits.
- Drift detector: for long-running streams, periodically compute running mean of softmax normalization constants; if the mean changes > delta over window W tokens, mark instability.
- KV provenance tag: attach a per-KV metadata bit that records "reduction_precision=bf16|fp32" so that when routing combines cached KVs with differently processed queries, we can detect precision mismatch and preemptively convert.

Proposed fallback protocol (deterministic, minimal scope):
Objective: Allow the request path to switch to higher-precision accumulation without requiring a full model reload or separate instance. Protocol steps: 
1) Detection: any of the heuristics above triggers a FallbackCandidate event. Record the event and telemetry sample.
2) Fast path conversion: if KV provenance tag indicates mismatch, perform a cheap upcast of affected cached KVs to fp32 on the GPU (in-place if memory format allows), and mark a route-scoped flag "precision_lock=fp32_reduction" for this request. This avoids recomputing KVs.
3) Kernel selection: choose kernels where accumulation/reduction axes are implemented in fp32 while preserving bf16 storage for weights and activations where safe (i.e., fp32 accumulation variant of GEMM, fp32 softmax accumulator, fp32 layernorm moments). Many vendor libraries expose this as a compile-time or runtime flag; our runtime will prefer specialized kernels via the kernel selector.
4) Token resumption: restart generation for the current request at the last consistent token boundary. The runtime must re-run the last attention step(s) that may have tainted state; we propose re-running the last 1–2 tokens depending on where detection occurred to bound latency.
5) Telemetry and adaptive policy: log event with deterministic tags (why triggered, which kernels switched, latency delta). If the same request pattern triggers fallback frequently, mark model+route for permanent precision_lock until model or weights are updated.

Notes on implementation complexity and perf tradeoffs:
- Upcasting KVs in-place is cheap relative to recomputing (memory transfer cost inside GPU memory and extra bytes stored). The kernel selector must support fp32 accumulation variants; we will maintain a small set of these kernels built and validated for our common hardware families.
- Restarting 1–2 tokens is an acceptable compromise in most interactive workloads; for low-latency streaming, we reduce window to 1 token. The heuristics should bias toward minimal restart distance.
- We must ensure fallback paths do not cause request deadlocks with scheduler autoscaling or burst policies. For example, dedicating a different kernel variant should not cause migration to a different device class mid-request. The fallback should be handled within the same device if possible.

Scheduler and batching considerations:
- Continuous batching increases the number of summands in reductions; consider a scheduler hint to limit effective batch sizes for requests flagged as "high dynamic range" (based on token statistics) to reduce accumulation error. This is a tunable knob: reduce batch cap by 1/2 for flagged requests.
- For mixed-precision sensitive models, allow a route-level config to opt-in to "precision-aware batching" which places requests with differing KV provenance or flagged instability into separate micro-batches. This reduces cross-request numeric contamination at minimal throughput cost.

Testing harness and reproduction steps (internal):
- Testbed setup: use the same GPU family used by customers (A100 and H100 families), driver versions pinned. Create a synthetic prompt generator that can: (a) inject extreme logit scalings, (b) simulate long stream concatenations, and (c) replay KV-provenance-mismatched sequences.
- Reproduction scripts: two entry points: reproduce_nan.sh (runs fused kernels in bf16 accumulation until NaN observed) and compare_fp32_fallback.sh (runs the same sequence with fallback kernels and asserts no NaN).
- Metrics to capture per run: token-latency p50/p95, additional memory bytes due to upcast, fallback frequency per 10k requests, average restart tokens. Log sample traces for internal triage.

Open questions / risks:
- Some vendor kernels do not expose per-axis accumulation precision control; for unsupported hardware we need emulation which may be too slow. Decision: maintain a compatibility matrix and fall back to an isolated fp32 execution path (higher latency) for unsupported devices.
- Telemetry noise: naive sampling may either miss rare NaNs or produce false positives. We will bootstrap thresholds conservatively and tune over staged rollout.
- Permanent precision locks reduce cost savings of mixed-precision. However, targeted locks are preferable to full fp32 deployments.

Action plan and rollout phases:
Phase 0 (prototype, infra-only): implement detection heuristics + telemetry. Build repro harness and evaluate on A100/H100. (Owner: Priya)
Phase 1 (kernel integration): add fp32-accumulation kernel variants to kernel selector, implement per-KV provenance tagging and fast upcast path. Add route config flags for precision-aware batching. (Owner: Diego)
Phase 2 (canary): rollout fallback protocol to internal canary fleet, monitor fallback frequency and latency hit. Tune sampling thresholds. (Owner: Hannah)
Phase 3 (gradual prod rollout): enable on small percentage of customer traffic with safe auto-disable on excessive latency impact. (Owner: eng-serving-runtime leads)

Appendix: quick examples and heuristics thresholds used in early tests:
- NaN sample short-circuit: sample_count=16. Any NaN -> immediate fallback.
- Dynamic range anomaly threshold: max/median > 1e5 (tunable; initial tests used 1e6 for fewer false positives).
- Drift window: W=256 tokens, delta=0.02 for normalized softmax constant mean.
- Restart token window: default 2 tokens, reduce to 1 for streaming routes.

Telemetry fields to emit on FallbackCandidate event:
- route_id, model_version, device_type, kernel_variant_from, kernel_variant_to, kv_provenance_tag, sample_count, detected_by (which heuristic), latency_before, latency_after, restart_tokens, fallback_reason_tag.

Conclusion:
Targeted fp32 accumulation fallbacks combined with lightweight detectors and KV provenance tagging provide a practical path to eliminate rare NaN and drift incidents without sacrificing the majority of bf16 performance benefits. Next steps are to deliver the prototype detection hooks and the kernel-selector plumbing for fp32-accumulation variants, then run a two-week canary to validate safety and tune thresholds.

Repro commands and links (internal):
- local repro: scripts/repro/reproduce_nan.sh --model gpt-like --seq 4096 --prompt-template stress-narrow-peaks
- fallback test: scripts/repro/compare_fp32_fallback.sh --device a100 --model gpt-like
- internal issue: JIRA:INF-912 (numeric drift incidents)

Notes to reviewers: please focus review on fallbacks that avoid full model recompute, and on whether restart token window sizes are acceptable for your routes. If you have kernel variants to contribute for other hardware families, add PRs to GH:redwood-inference/runtime#1873.
